title: The Tree That Saved Our Playground

pages.text: At midday break, the sun shone brightly over the school playground. Seven-year-old Kwame and his friend Abena wanted to play ampe, but the bare dusty ground felt hot under their sandals. ‘Phew!’ said Kwame, wiping his forehead. ‘The sunny side of the yard is too hot today!’
sentences: At midday break, the sun shone brightly over the school playground.
Seven-year-old Kwame and his friend Abena wanted to play ampe, but the bare dusty ground felt hot under their sandals.
‘Phew!’ said Kwame, wiping his forehead.
‘The sunny side of the yard is too hot today!’
pages.alt: Kwame and Abena stand on the sunny, dusty side of their school playground wiping their foreheads under the bright sun.

pages.text: Across the yard stood One Big Neem Tree with wide green branches. All the children ran under its leafy roof. Underneath the tree, the ground felt cool and a gentle breeze touched their cheeks. ‘Why is it so much cooler under the tree?’ asked Abena.
sentences: Across the yard stood One Big Neem Tree with wide green branches.
All the children ran under its leafy roof.
Underneath the tree, the ground felt cool and a gentle breeze touched their cheeks.
‘Why is it so much cooler under the tree?’ asked Abena.
pages.alt: Kwame, Abena and their classmates stand comfortably in the wide green shade of a large neem tree.

pages.text: Their teacher, Madam Akua, walked over holding two safe red-liquid thermometers. ‘Let us investigate like scientists!’ she smiled. They placed one thermometer on a shaded bench under the neem tree, and the second thermometer on a bench out in the direct sunshine.
sentences: Their teacher, Madam Akua, walked over holding two safe red-liquid thermometers.
‘Let us investigate like scientists!’ she smiled.
They placed one thermometer on a shaded bench under the neem tree, and the second thermometer on a bench out in the direct sunshine.
pages.alt: Madam Akua shows Kwame and Abena two red-liquid classroom thermometers to compare the shade and the sun.

pages.text: After ten minutes, they checked both thermometers. Out in the sun, the red line had climbed high, to thirty-six degrees! Under the neem tree, the red line stayed much lower, at thirty degrees. ‘The tree made the air six degrees cooler!’ cheered Kwame.
sentences: After ten minutes, they checked both thermometers.
Out in the sun, the red line had climbed high, to thirty-six degrees!
Under the neem tree, the red line stayed much lower, at thirty degrees.
‘The tree made the air six degrees cooler!’ cheered Kwame.
pages.alt: Kwame and Abena look closely at the two thermometers, seeing the lower red line in the shade.

pages.text: ‘How does a tree cool the playground without a fan or electricity?’ asked Abena, touching a rough brown root. ‘In two clever ways,’ said Madam Akua. ‘First, the thick green leaves block the sun’s hot rays from baking the soil. That gives us shade.’
sentences: ‘How does a tree cool the playground without a fan or electricity?’ asked Abena, touching a rough brown root.
‘In two clever ways,’ said Madam Akua.
‘First, the thick green leaves block the sun’s hot rays from baking the soil.
That gives us shade.’
pages.alt: Abena touches the trunk while looking up at the thick green canopy blocking the bright sunbeams.

pages.text: ‘Second,’ said Madam Akua, ‘roots drink water from the soil and send it up to the leaves. The leaves release tiny invisible drops of water vapour into the air. As that water evaporates, it cools the air around the tree, just like water cooling your skin after you wash your hands!’
sentences: ‘Second,’ said Madam Akua, ‘roots drink water from the soil and send it up to the leaves.
The leaves release tiny invisible drops of water vapour into the air.
As that water evaporates, it cools the air around the tree, just like water cooling your skin after you wash your hands!’
pages.alt: Madam Akua points from the tree’s roots up the trunk to the green leaves in the breeze.

pages.text: Kwame looked back at the bare, hot side of the playground. ‘One tree cannot shade the whole school,’ he said. ‘Can we plant more trees so everyone has cool shade?’ ‘Yes!’ said Madam Akua. The next morning, the class worked as a team to dig holes, plant four young mango and neem saplings, and spread dry leaves around them as mulch to keep the soil damp.
sentences: Kwame looked back at the bare, hot side of the playground.
‘One tree cannot shade the whole school,’ he said.
‘Can we plant more trees so everyone has cool shade?’ ‘Yes!’ said Madam Akua.
The next morning, the class worked as a team to dig holes, plant four young mango and neem saplings, and spread dry leaves around them as mulch to keep the soil damp.
pages.alt: Kwame, Abena and their classmates work together digging, planting young saplings, and watering them with watering cans.

pages.text: Every morning before class, Team Green gave the young saplings a drink of water and built small wooden guards to protect them from goats. Soon, shiny new leaves sprouted on every sapling! ‘One day,’ smiled Abena, ‘children who come after us will play in the cool shade we planted together.’ The end.

activities.question: What did Kwame and Abena discover when they checked the two thermometers?
options: The air under the neem tree was six degrees cooler than the air in the hot sun
It was hotter under the tree than in the sun
Trees make the playground darker at night
activities.explanation: The thermometer in the sun read 36 degrees while the thermometer in the shade read 30 degrees—6 degrees cooler!

activities.question: What are the two ways a tree cools the playground?
options: Leaves block hot sunbeams for shade and release cooling water vapour
It plugs into a wall socket and spins its branches like a fan
It drops ice cubes onto the grass every afternoon
It pushes the sun behind a mountain
activities.explanation: Tree leaves block direct sunlight (shade) and release moisture from the soil that evaporates and cools the air.

activities.definition: A tool used to measure how hot or cold something is.
distractors: A bucket used to carry soil
A wooden fence around a young tree

activities.prompt: Which words start with the sh sound, like shade?
Why did the children spread dry leaves (mulch) around the base of the young saplings and build wooden guards?
Put the playground story in order.
items: The bare playground feels too hot in the midday sun.
Madam Akua and the class measure the temperature in the sun and in the shade.
The children learn how leaves block sunlight and release cooling moisture.
The class plants and waters four new saplings together.

activities.prompt: How does it feel to plant and care for a tree that will help other children in the future?

glossary.definition: A cool, darker area where something blocks direct sunlight.
An instrument that measures temperature, how hot or cold the air is.
Turns from liquid water into invisible water vapour in the air, which cools the surface.
Young, small trees that are growing.
A layer of dry leaves or grass spread over soil to keep moisture in.
